summary: Research how react-scan/react-grab achieve drop-in install and what a canvas-focused equivalent would take

reactScan.how_dropin_works: Install is either an unpkg script tag (`<script crossOrigin="anonymous" src="//unpkg.com/react-scan/dist/auto.global.js">`) pasted "before any scripts" in index.html, or an equivalent early import for bundler setups (Next.js `strategy="beforeInteractive"` in app/layout.tsx or Pages Router _document.tsx; Next 15.3+ `instrumentation-client.ts`; Vite: first line of main.tsx). `npx react-scan@latest init` automates picking the right variant. There is zero app-code change because the mechanism doesn't touch React's API surface at all — it exploits a hook React already calls unconditionally: `window.__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__`. React's reconciler checks for this global and, if present, calls `hook.inject(renderer)` on renderer registration and `hook.onCommitFiberRoot(rendererID, root)` on every commit — this is the exact mechanism React DevTools uses, and it requires no cooperation from application code. `auto.global.js` runs `import 'bippy'` as its very first statement (before importing react-scan's own `./index`), and bippy's module-load side effect (`safelyInstallRDTHook` → `getRDTHook` → `installRDTHook`) synchronously `Object.defineProperty`-installs a fake hook object with a no-op `inject`/`onCommitFiberRoot`/etc. onto `globalThis` if none exists yet. Because this happens as an unconditional side effect the moment the script parses, and script tags placed 'before any scripts' or bundler entries placed at the top of main.tsx guarantee it runs before React's own bundle executes, React finds the hook already sitting there and calls into it exactly as it would for the real DevTools extension — react-scan is just intercepting that existing contract. WHAT HAPPENS IF REACT LOADS FIRST: React's reconciler does its own hook-presence check once at module init and, if `__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__` is absent at that moment, some code paths simply skip wiring commit callbacks for that renderer permanently (this is why the README/bippy README both say the import order is 'critical' and must be first). If a hook already exists (e.g., the real React DevTools browser extension got there first, or bippy runs a second time), bippy's `patchRDTHook` instead wraps the existing hook's `inject`/`onCommitFiberRoot`/etc. in place (composable dispatcher pattern) rather than replacing it, so it can still work — just less reliably, since it depends on React not having already skipped hook attachment. `installRDTHook` also monkey-patches `window.hasOwnProperty` as a defensive hack so that if the real React DevTools extension's own installer runs afterward and does `if (!window.hasOwnProperty('__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__'))`, it still thinks no hook exists and won't skip its own install, letting both coexist.
reactScan.core_mechanism: Render detection: on every `onCommitFiberRoot(rendererID, root)` callback (fired once per React commit, i.e., once per completed render+DOM-mutation batch), react-scan's `createInstrumentation` (packages/scan/src/core/instrumentation.ts) calls bippy's `traverseRenderedFibers(root.current, callback)`. That function is a Suspense-aware, mount/update/unmount-classifying walk of the current vs. alternate fiber trees (ported from React DevTools backend's own renderer logic — it explicitly compares `wasMounted`/`isMounted` via `fiber.memoizedState.element`, and separately handles Suspense primary/fallback tree transitions) and calls back with every fiber that actually rendered, tagged 'mount'|'update'|'unmount'. For each such fiber, react-scan collects props/state/context changes via bippy's `traverseProps`/`traverseState`(via a wrapper `getStateChanges`)/`traverseContexts`, timing via `getTimings` (reads `fiber.actualDuration`, which React's profiler-instrumented dev build populates on every fiber, split into self vs total time by subtracting children's durations), and a stable numeric id via `getFiberId` (a WeakMap-backed identity since fiber objects are recreated every render). Unnecessary-render detection is react-scan's own addition on top of bippy's primitives, not something bippy provides: `isRenderUnnecessary(fiber)` (core/instrumentation.ts) first checks bippy's `didFiberCommit` (reads React's own fiber `flags`/`subtreeFlags` bitmask against a `MutationMask` of Placement|Update|ChildDeletion|ContentReset|Hydrating|Visibility|Snapshot — i.e., 'did this fiber or its subtree actually touch the DOM'); if nothing committed it's trivially unnecessary. Otherwise it walks `getMutatedHostFibers(fiber)` (bippy: DFS down to committed host/DOM fibers) and for each, calls bippy's `traverseProps` to diff every prop key between `fiber.memoizedProps` and `fiber.alternate.memoizedProps`. A prop counts as a 'required' (necessary) change only if `!isEqual(prev,next)` (react-scan's own `isEqual` = SameValueZero, i.e. `===` plus NaN handling — pure reference equality, not deep) AND `!isValueUnstable(prev,next)`. `isValueUnstable` is the actual 'unnecessary render' heuristic: it runs both values through `fastSerialize` (react-scan's own cheap structural summarizer — arrays become `[length]`, plain objects become `{keyCount}`, React elements become `<Type propCount>`, functions become their `.toString()`, everything else its constructor name) and, if the two serialized strings match AND both values are `typeof 'function'|'object'`, treats it as 'same shape, different reference' — the classic `onClick={() => ...}` / `style={{...}}` inline-literal case from the README — and therefore not a real change. If zero props required a change across all mutated host descendants, the whole render is flagged unnecessary. This heuristic is intentionally shallow/approximate (structural counts, not deep-equal), and in the current `main` snapshot the feature is gated off by a hardcoded `const TRACK_UNNECESSARY_RENDERS = false` with a `// re-implement this in new-outlines` TODO — it exists in source but isn't live by default right now. Division of labor: bippy supplies the hook install/patch, the mount/update/unmount fiber-tree walker, generic prop/state/context traversal, the commit/mutation bitflag readers, timing/displayName/type/id extraction, and React's own fiber-tag constants; react-scan supplies the unnecessary-render classifier (fastSerialize/isValueUnstable/isRenderUnnecessary), change aggregation into typed `Change`/`ChangeReason` records, FPS tracking, and everything visual.
key_dependencies: bippy (^0.5.39, same author) — installs/patches window.__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__, provides instrument()/traverseRenderedFibers/traverseProps/traverseState/traverseContexts/didFiberCommit/getMutatedHostFibers/getTimings/getFiberId/getDisplayName and React's fiber-tag constants; this is the entire 'talk to React internals' layer
@preact/signals (^2.9.0) — reactive state (isPaused, options, store) driving both the instrumentation pause/resume and the toolbar UI without a React re-render dependency
preact (^10.29.1) — the entire toolbar/notifications/inspector UI is written in Preact, not React, so react-scan's own UI doesn't get caught by (or interfere with) the React tree it's instrumenting
OffscreenCanvas + Web Worker (native browser APIs, no library) — moves the outline-overlay draw loop off the main thread when supported
SharedArrayBuffer/ArrayBuffer + Float32Array (native) — packs outline rect data (id, count, x, y, width, height, didCommit) for zero-copy-ish postMessage to the worker
IntersectionObserver (native) — batches getBoundingClientRect-equivalent rect resolution for many DOM elements without synchronous layout thrashing, and naturally skips off-screen elements

@babel/core, unplugin, es-module-lexer — power the separate react-component-name sub-package (a build-time plugin, Vite/Webpack/esbuild/rspack/rolldown/rollup/astro/loader variants, that names otherwise-anonymous components), not part of the render-detection core
commander, prompts, picocolors — the `react-scan init` CLI installer that auto-detects the framework and wires up the script tag/import
reactScan.core_complexity: Essential render-detection + overlay core is roughly 1,500–2,000 lines of load-bearing TypeScript inside react-scan itself (core/instrumentation.ts ~400 lines; core/index.ts wiring/options/production-gating; new-outlines/ canvas.ts + offscreen-canvas.worker.ts + index.ts ~1,000 lines, of which the genuinely hard bits — lerp/fade animation, rect merging, label-collision merging, worker/SharedArrayBuffer packing — are maybe 150–250 lines, the rest is DOM/worker plumbing). Add bippy's own core.ts (~1,260 lines) and rdt-hook.ts (~220 lines) — architecturally part of the same 'detect renders' engine even though it ships as a separate package — and the full render-detection+draw pipeline is on the order of 3,000 lines total, of which the parts that required non-obvious knowledge of undocumented React internals (the hook-install-before-React trick and its hasOwnProperty defensive hack, the Suspense-aware mount/update/unmount fiber-tree walker adapted from DevTools' own backend, the fiber flags/subtreeFlags mutation-bitmask reads, the unnecessary-render prop-diff heuristic) are a few hundred lines at most. By contrast, the polish is the majority of the repo by volume: web/ (toolbar, floating draggable widget with fps meter, notifications panel with bar charts/slowdown history/'optimize' suggestions, component-tree inspector, props diff viewer, flash-on-select overlay) is 60 files / ~442KB — roughly 4-5x the size of core/ (13 files / ~96KB) and new-outlines/ (4 files / ~29KB) combined. There's also a whole separate react-component-name bundler-plugin package (~54KB across 24 files, Babel/esbuild/webpack/rspack/rolldown/rollup/astro variants) that's tangential polish (naming anonymous components at build time), plus a CLI installer (~43KB) and a 'lite' variant (~79KB). So the ratio is roughly 1 part hard/essential mechanism to 4+ parts UI/tooling polish by code volume.
reusable_pieces: bippy itself (npm, MIT) — the whole 'pretend to be React DevTools, get commit callbacks + fiber diffing utilities' engine (instrument, traverseRenderedFibers, traverseProps/State/Contexts, didFiberCommit/didFiberRender, getMutatedHostFibers, getTimings, hasMemoCache, getDisplayName/getType, setFiberId/getFiberId) is designed to be depended on directly rather than reimplemented; it claims to work across React 17-19 (its own README's wording — narrower than react-scan's package.json peerDependency range of 16.8-19, worth verifying for a target React 16 use case)
bippy/install-hook-only (~90 bytes) — install just the devtools-hook stub and hand-roll your own fiber utilities from bippy/core if bundle size matters more than convenience

the getBatchedRectMap IntersectionObserver-generator pattern (new-outlines/index.ts) — a generic, React-agnostic technique for resolving many elements' rects cheaply without forced synchronous layout and while skipping off-screen ones; directly liftable for any DOM-highlighting tool

the OffscreenCanvas+Worker+SharedArrayBuffer overlay pipeline (new-outlines/canvas.ts + offscreen-canvas.worker.ts) — zero React-specific logic, pure 'animate fading/lerping highlight rectangles with merged labels over arbitrary screen coordinates'; portable wholesale to a different instrumentation source

fastSerialize / isValueUnstable (core/instrumentation.ts) — a small, standalone 'same shape but different reference' heuristic useful for any unnecessary-render or memoization-audit tool, independent of the rest of react-scan's machinery

NOT worth lifting: the Preact toolbar/notifications/inspector UI (60 files, tightly coupled to react-scan's own signals-based store), the CLI framework auto-detect installer, and the separate react-component-name bundler-plugin package — all bespoke and much larger than the mechanism itself
reactScan.notes: React version support: package.json peerDependencies are `react`/`react-dom` `^16.8.0 || ^17.0.0 || ^18.0.0 || ^19.0.0`, but bippy's own README claims support only for 'modern react (v17-19)' — a narrower, slightly inconsistent claim worth confirming empirically before relying on React 16 support. Production behavior: `getIsProduction()` calls bippy's `detectReactBuildType` (checks `renderer.bundleType`), and `start()` is a no-op in production builds unless the user opts in via `dangerouslyForceRunInProduction` (explicitly documented as 'not recommended') — this exists because minified/production React doesn't reliably expose the profiling timings (`fiber.actualDuration`) or full displayNames the tool depends on. `getIsProduction` also deliberately never caches a `true` (production) verdict, only a `false` one, because tools like the Next.js dev overlay can register a second, later-arriving dev renderer alongside a production one. The DOM overlay is browser/canvas-specific (isClientEnvironment checks `window.document.createElement`), so on React Native only the fiber-data layer (via bippy) applies, not the visual outline layer. In the current `main` snapshot, the 'unnecessary render' classification is present in source but hardcoded off (`const TRACK_UNNECESSARY_RENDERS = false`, with a `// re-implement this in new-outlines` comment and a `// FIXME: calculation is slow` note on `isRenderUnnecessary` itself) — so it's mid-refactor/disabled by default right now, not a stable always-on feature; anyone reading the source today should not assume the red-outline-for-unnecessary-renders behavior is currently wired up end to end. No dedicated 'architecture' doc or author blog post was found linked from either repo's README (searched both aidenybai/react-scan and aidenybai/bippy); everything above was reverse-engineered directly from source (packages/scan/src/core/instrumentation.ts, packages/scan/src/new-outlines/*, packages/bippy/src/{core,rdt-hook}.ts) plus the two READMEs. The user's premise that there's a 'replay' feature was not found in the source tree — the closest thing is the notifications panel's slowdown-history/optimize-suggestions views, not a session replay.

reactGrab.how_dropin_works: Two install paths, both zero-app-code-change: (1) `npx grab@latest init` — a separate CLI package that detects the framework (Next.js App/Pages router, Vite, Webpack) and auto-inserts the right snippet, plus drops an agent-skill file (`skills/react-grab/SKILL.md`) so coding agents know the paste format. (2) Manual: a dev-only `<Script src="//unpkg.com/react-grab/dist/index.global.js" strategy="beforeInteractive">` tag (Next.js) or a conditional `if (import.meta.env.DEV) import('react-grab')` (Vite/Webpack). Either way, `react-grab`'s entry module (`src/index.ts`) is a pure side-effect module: on load it checks `window.__REACT_GRAB_DISABLED__`, checks for an existing global instance (dedup across nested iframes via `getParentReactGrabApi`), and otherwise calls `init()` immediately, stores the result at `window.__REACT_GRAB__`, and fires a `react-grab:init` CustomEvent. `init()` merges options from a `data-options` JSON script-tag attribute with programmatic options, wires up a Solid reactive store + plugin registry with a single AbortController for teardown, and lazily `import()`s the actual overlay UI so the interaction-detection logic can be ready before the heavier rendering code parses. The overlay mounts into an `open` Shadow DOM host (`position:fixed;inset:0;pointer-events:none`) appended to `<body>` (deferred to DOMContentLoaded if body isn't parsed yet, since appending during `<Script strategy=\"beforeInteractive\">` throws hydration errors; re-appended via `setTimeout` to survive React/Next hydration wiping the subtree and to win z-index fights with other tools like react-scan). Nothing in the app's own React tree needs to change — there's no provider, no wrapper component; the tool observes the app from outside via bippy.
reactGrab.core_mechanism: Entirely built on `bippy` (hard dependency `bippy: ^0.6.1`, same author, bippy.dev), NOT on the user having the React DevTools browser extension installed. bippy's `rdt-hook.ts` runs before React itself and checks `window.__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__`; if it's absent, bippy installs its own stub via `Object.defineProperty(globalThis, '__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__', {get/set...})` that mimics the real hook's shape (`inject`, `onCommitFiberRoot`, `renderers: Map`, etc.), and it temporarily patches `window.hasOwnProperty` so a real DevTools extension installing later doesn't get blocked and instead merges into bippy's tracking (`patchRDTHook`). Because every React renderer unconditionally calls `hook.inject(rendererObject)` on startup (this is built into react-dom itself, extension or not), the stub hook captures the renderer object — giving access to `ReactCurrentDispatcher`/`currentDispatcherRef`, `findFiberByHostInstance`, and per-commit `onCommitFiberRoot`/`onCommitFiberUnmount` callbacks — the same channel the real DevTools extension uses, self-installed. Element→fiber: `getFiberFromHostInstance()` first tries `renderer.findFiberByHostInstance(node)`; falling back, it reads the DOM node's own React-stamped property (`__reactFiber$<hash>` / `__reactContainer$<hash>` / `__reactInternalInstance$<hash>`, caching which key name worked), then falls back further to walking tracked fiber roots comparing `stateNode === hostInstance`. Fiber→component stack: bippy's `getOwnerStack()` branches on React version — React 19+ fibers carry a `_debugStack` Error whose `.stack` is parsed between `react-stack-top-frame`/`react-stack-bottom-frame` sentinels; React 17–18 lack that, so bippy re-invokes each composite fiber's render function/constructor with hooks disabled and console silenced, diffs the resulting stack against a "control" stack thrown at the same call site, and extracts the differing frame — the same trick React DevTools itself uses internally. Fiber→file/line: those frames point at bundled output, so bippy's `symbolicateStack` fetches the bundle, finds `//# sourceMappingURL=`, decodes it via `@jridgewell/sourcemap-codec`, and resolves the original position (WeakRef-cached). react-grab layers Next.js RSC-specific enrichment on top in its own `core/context.ts` (`enrichServerFrameLocations`/`symbolicateServerFrames`, POSTing to Next's dev-only `/__nextjs_original-stack-frames` endpoint to resolve `rsc://` virtual URLs), plus its own display-name filter lists (Next.js internal wrappers, React built-ins, `motion.`/`styled.`/etc. prefixes) and a "context line budget" that caps how many stack frames get copied. Props/state values are never extracted — confirmed by grepping `context.ts`/`generate-snippet.ts`/copy plugin for `memoizedProps`/`memoizedState` (zero hits). The default copy action (`formatElementInfo`) is just `getHTMLPreview(element) + composeElementContext(traceContext)` — DOM tag/attributes plus the resolved component/source trace, nothing from React's internal props or state.
key_dependencies: bippy (^0.6.1) — does all the actual fiber-tree access, owner-stack reconstruction, and source-map symbolication; react-grab is a UI/UX layer on top of it
solid-js — the overlay UI framework (setup-once reactive components, not React, to avoid re-render coupling with the host app)
@jridgewell/trace-mapping / sourcemap-codec (via bippy) — source map decoding for symbolication
tailwindcss (build-time) — compiles react-grab's own overlay styles, shipped as a separate dist/styles.css
@react-grab/cli (workspace dep) — the npx grab init installer, separate package
reactGrab.core_complexity: The genuinely hard core — dispatcher/update-queue patching to freeze React state (`freeze-updates.ts`), 4-system animation freezing (CSS, SVG SMIL, WAAPI, GSAP), owner-stack reconstruction + symbolication (mostly reused from bippy, not reimplemented), RSC frame enrichment, and KeyboardEvent.prototype.key patching for shortcut claiming — is maybe 2–3k LOC of genuinely fragile, version-sensitive internals-patching; the architecture doc itself says this "will need to change as React's internals evolve." Everything else — the SolidJS canvas overlay with OffscreenCanvas-layer compositing and RAF-lerped bounds, the toolbar/context-menu/hierarchy-menu system, the live CSS/Tailwind edit panel (color picker, value stepper, property search/recommendation), Three.js/react-three-fiber and Solid source-location support, iframe/shadow-DOM traversal, drag multi-select, touch mode, the plugin registry, and a whole separate CLI package with native clipboard readers in Swift/PowerShell — is polish and surface-area breadth, roughly 80%+ of the ~800 tracked files (150+ e2e specs alone). Rough split: ~15–20% hard core (freeze + source-resolution + init), the rest is UI/editor/multi-framework/CLI/test surface.
reusable_pieces: bippy itself (standalone npm package, MIT) — getRDTHook/installRDTHook for DevTools-hook-free fiber access, getFiberFromHostInstance, getOwnerStack, symbolicateStack, normalizeFileName; this is the exact 'DOM element -> component name + source' building block
react-grab/primitives sub-export — getElementAtPoint, isElementGrabbable, hit-testing/filtering, clipboard, editor-open helpers; explicitly designed by the maintainers for 'build your own React Grab'
The freeze subsystem (freeze-updates.ts, freeze-animations.ts, freeze-pseudo-states.ts, freeze-gsap.ts) as a standalone 'pause the live page for inspection' toolkit, independent of the picker UI

The Shadow-DOM host-mounting pattern in mount-root.ts (fixed pointer-events:none host, open shadow root, re-append-on-timeout to survive hydration/z-index wars) — solid pattern for any dev-tool overlay injected into an arbitrary host page
KeyboardEvent.prototype.key getter patching to 'claim' a shortcut from the host app without relying on stopPropagation (unreliable under React's synthetic event delegation)
The open-in-editor pipeline: try the dev server's own endpoint (Vite /__open-in-editor, Next /__nextjs_launch-editor) and fall back to a hosted vscode://file/... redirect
The plugin-registry hook-dispatch pattern (callHook / callHookWithHandled / callHookReduce) — a small, clean design for making a copy/inspect pipeline externally extensible
reactGrab.notes: Two things worth flagging back: (1) react-grab is not primarily a 'grab props/state' tool — it's DOM-attribute + source-location context, which is a materially different (and much cheaper to reproduce) core than what the task framing implied. (2) The self-installing DevTools-hook trick in bippy means this works without the user having the React DevTools browser extension, but it's fundamentally reading React's undocumented internals (fiber shape, dispatcher location, _debugStack format) — the maintainers' own docs call the approach 'inherently fragile' and expect it to break across React versions. Bundle-fetch-based symbolication (refetching the JS bundle client-side to find its sourcemap comment) is a real perf/CSP consideration for anyone reusing this — it's a network call per unique bundle URL, not a build-time step.

canvas_instrumentation_techniques: Monkey-patch CanvasRenderingContext2D.prototype / WebGLRenderingContext.prototype (and WebGL2RenderingContext.prototype) methods: wrap every draw-affecting method (fillRect, drawImage, fill, stroke, putImageData, drawArrays, drawElements, clear, etc.) to increment a per-frame counter and accumulate self-time via performance.now() deltas around the original call. This is the technique used by tools like Rob--W/canvas-interceptor and canvas-sequencer: wrapObject() iterates the prototype and replaces each function with a logging wrapper, storing call args/logs on the context or canvas element (e.g. a __proxyLogs array). A Proxy over the context object is the cleaner modern equivalent to manual per-method wrapping and handles get/apply uniformly, at the cost of an extra indirection per property access.

Wrap HTMLCanvasElement.prototype.getContext itself (patch before any app code runs) so every 2D/webgl/webgl2 context handed out is already instrumented, rather than requiring each call site to opt in. This is the standard 'install before app boots' pattern — inject the patch as an early <script> or a module imported first — and is what lets a drop-in tool avoid modifying app/library canvas code at all.

requestAnimationFrame loop timing: wrap window.requestAnimationFrame to bracket each frame, recording rAF-to-rAF delta (frame time / implied FPS), and reset the per-frame draw-call counters/timers at the top of each rAF callback so counts are attributable to a single frame rather than accumulating across frames indefinitely.

performance.mark/performance.measure around draw batches (e.g. mark('canvas-draw-start') ... mark('canvas-draw-end') ... measure('canvas-draw', ...)) to get entries visible in the Chrome Performance panel's 'Timings' track, which is useful for correlating canvas work with React's own scheduling/commit marks if React is built with the profiling bundle. Overhead is small but non-zero (~0.65us/mark, ~0.85us/measure per Paul Irish's benchmark) so mark-per-draw-call (thousands/frame) can itself become the bottleneck; mark-per-frame or per-batch is safer.

GPU-side timing via EXT_disjoint_timer_query (WebGL1) / EXT_disjoint_timer_query_webgl2: insert timer queries into the GPU command queue around draw calls, since CPU-side call duration for gl.draw* calls is near-zero (commands are just enqueued) and does not reflect actual GPU execution time. Chrome desktop only (>=70), removed then reintroduced due to a security disclosure; results can be 'disjoint' (invalid) if the GPU changed clock/power state mid-measurement, so every read must check the DISJOINT flag before trusting the value. For WebGPU, the equivalent is the 'timestamp-query' optional feature.

OffscreenCanvas caveats for instrumentation: if rendering is moved to a Worker via canvas.transferControlToOffscreen(), the main-thread monkey-patches never see the calls — the wrapping has to happen inside the worker, and cross-thread correlation to React state (which lives on the main thread) requires an explicit message-passing bridge (postMessage timestamps) rather than direct call interception. Also, rAF inside a worker fires on its own schedule tied to the worker's rendering, and multiple queued rAF callbacks in the same worker tick share one timestamp, which flattens per-callback timing unless you also timestamp with performance.now() manually inside the callback body.

Command-stream capture (not just counting): record each draw call's full argument list into a per-frame array to reconstruct 'what was drawn' rather than just 'how much was drawn' — this is what canvas-interceptor's getCanvasReplay() and Spector.js's per-frame command list do, and it's the prerequisite for redundant-frame detection (you need the actual command list, not just a count, to compare frames).
attribution_approaches: Correlate via the React DevTools global hook (__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__): register onCommitFiberRoot on window.__REACT_DEVTOOLS_GLOBAL_HOOK__.onCommitFiberRoot (or inject a listener before React DevTools' own extension attaches) to get a callback with the fiber root and commit priority/timestamp on every commit. Because this hook exists in dev builds and, if you alias react-dom to react-dom/profiling, in production too, it's the standard non-invasive way to know 'a commit just happened' without modifying app code. The gap: this alone tells you commits happened, not which commit caused a specific canvas draw — you need to pair it with a timing window.

Timestamp-window correlation: record the commit timestamp from onCommitFiberRoot (or from a <Profiler onRender> callback, which is the officially supported, production-safe surface and gives id/phase/actualDuration/startTime/commitTime) and separately record the timestamp of each instrumented canvas draw batch (from the rAF-loop timing above). Attribute a draw batch to a commit if the draw batch's start falls within some small delta after commitTime and before the next rAF fires — effectively bucketing canvas work by the commit that most recently preceded it in the same macrotask/microtask window. This is a heuristic (no hard causal link exists between 'commit finished' and 'a useEffect drew to canvas'), but it's the approach implicit in how most 'commit -> paint' correlation tools work since React itself doesn't expose a causal pointer from a fiber to arbitrary imperative side effects like canvas writes.

Stack capture inside the patched canvas methods: at the moment a draw call fires, capture `new Error().stack` (or `Error.captureStackTrace` on V8) and parse it for the nearest recognizable component/hook frame (e.g. a component name embedded via a named function, or a custom hook like useCanvasDraw that always appears in the trace). This directly attributes a draw call to source code without needing React internals, but is fragile: production/minified builds strip names, arrow functions in hooks often produce anonymous frames, and capturing a stack per draw call (thousands/frame) is expensive enough to skew the very measurement you're taking — so this is best used sampled (e.g. 1 in N frames) or only for the first draw call of a batch.

React component stack via componentStack (as surfaced in error boundaries / componentDidCatch, or programmatically via the same internal machinery React DevTools uses) gives an accurate component-tree path but is normally only available inside an error boundary's catch, not on-demand at an arbitrary point in time — so it's attribution-after-a-crash, not attribution-of-a-frame, unless you reach into React's internal current-owner tracking (unstable, version-fragile).

Owner/currentOwner tracking: React DevTools' backend and profiler resolve 'which component instance is currently rendering' via ReactCurrentOwner / equivalent internals exposed through the DevTools hook's renderer interface (getFiberRoots, findFiberByHostInstance, etc.). A dev tool could tap the same renderer interface DevTools uses (documented informally via the react-devtools-extensions and react-reconciler source) to walk from a DOM/canvas host instance back up to the owning component fiber, then tag any draw call issued synchronously during that fiber's render/commit as attributable to it. This is how tools like react-render-tracker attribute renders to fibers, though none of the surveyed tools extend that attribution into canvas draw calls specifically — that link (fiber -> canvas draw) is the actual gap to fill for this project.

Manual instrumentation surface (opt-in, most reliable): rather than inferring attribution, expose a small onPerfTiming-style prop/context (as already scoped in project_metrics_graph_perf_scope for MetricsGraphCanvas) that the drawing component itself calls with its own identity — trading 'automatic drop-in' for 'zero ambiguity,' useful as a ground-truth channel to validate the heuristic-based automatic attribution above.
existing_tools: Spector.js (BabylonJS/Spector.js) — hooks WebGL1/WebGL2 context creation and every GL call, capturing the full command list, associated state, and textures for one captured frame; ships as a browser extension (Chrome/Firefox) and a standalone/npm library you can embed. Very drop-in for WebGL (single script include, click 'capture'), and its per-frame command-list capture is directly reusable for the 'compare successive frames' redundancy check. What it lacks for this use case: zero React awareness (no commit/fiber correlation, no notion of 'component'), and it's WebGL-only — a 2D canvas app (e.g. Canvas2D chart rendering, likely what MetricsGraphCanvas/LineChart uses per prior project notes) gets nothing from it.

figma/webgl-profiler — GPU-side profiler using EXT_disjoint_timer_query with pushContext()/popContext()/withContext() manual annotation calls that produce a flamechart viewable in speedscope.app. Closest existing prior art to 'a real perf tool built by a product team for their own canvas-heavy app.' Drop-in-ness is low: it requires the app to manually annotate GPU work with named context regions (not automatic), Chrome-desktop-only, and has known hardware/driver crash bugs. No React integration at all — annotation is manual per call site, which is the opposite of the 'drop-in' goal here but validates GPU-timing-via-timer-query as sound for a 2D/WebGL hybrid tool.

why-did-you-render — monkey-patches React.createElement and injects a hook into every component (historically via the internals symbol __SECRET_INTERNALS_DO_NOT_USE_OR_YOU_WILL_BE_FIRED) to diff props/state/context between renders and warn on 'avoidable' re-renders. Extremely drop-in for React re-render detection (one import + whyDidYouRender(React, opts)), but has zero awareness of canvas or imperative side effects — it only sees React's own render/props diffing, not what a component's useEffect subsequently painted to a canvas. A component can be flagged as 're-rendering unnecessarily' by WDYR while its canvas draw is actually fine (memoized inside the effect), or vice versa — it's an orthogonal signal, not a substitute.

react-render-tracker (lahmatiy) — a standalone DevTools-style panel that uses the same React DevTools backend hook infrastructure to build a timeline of mounts/updates/unmounts per fiber and the reasons for each update, positioned as a complement to React DevTools rather than a replacement. Drop-in via a script/extension, no source changes needed. Like WDYR, it stops at the React render boundary — it has no model of canvas commands or GPU work, so a component that re-renders zero times but redraws its canvas every animation frame (a common bug shape: rAF loop inside a ref callback, decoupled from React's render cycle) is invisible to it.

React DevTools Profiler (official, react-devtools-extensions / <Profiler> component) — the <Profiler onRender> component is the only one of these surveyed tools that's production-safe and officially supported; gives per-subtree actualDuration/baseDuration/commitTime. It's the natural timestamp source for the 'timestamp-window correlation' attribution approach above. Misses: no canvas/GPU visibility whatsoever, and actualDuration is 0 outside profiling builds unless react-dom/profiling is aliased in, which has its own bundle-size/perf cost in production.

Chrome DevTools Performance panel — records a full main-thread flame chart plus a GPU track, screenshots per frame, and automatically flags Long Tasks (>50ms). performance.mark/measure entries you emit show up in the 'Timings' track alongside this, which is the cheapest way to eyeball-correlate 'React commit here' vs 'canvas draw there' without building custom tooling. What it lacks as a 'drop-in dev tool': it's a manual, one-recording-at-a-time human workflow, not a live always-on redundancy detector, and it has no concept of 'this draw call was identical to the last one' — that comparison is left entirely to the person reading the flame chart.

KonvaJS Devtools (Chrome extension) — adds a Konva-specific panel to inspect/profile a Konva.js scene graph, analogous to React DevTools but for Konva's own retained-mode canvas layer, and Konva itself does built-in dirty-region/layer-based redraw minimization. Relevant only if the underlying canvas library is Konva; irrelevant to raw Canvas2D/WebGL app code or to any other charting lib, and again has no React commit correlation.

react-scan — detects 'unnecessary renders' by diffing actual DOM output pre/post-render (trackUnnecessaryRenders option) and can optionally use OffscreenCanvas + a Web Worker just to render its own highlight overlays off the main thread (that OffscreenCanvas use is react-scan's own UI, not an instrumentation target). Extremely drop-in (script tag or npm, no code changes). Its redundant-render detection logic (structural DOM diff after render) is conceptually the closest existing pattern to 'redundant canvas redraw detection,' but it's built for the DOM, not canvas — the equivalent for canvas would be diffing the draw-command stream instead of DOM nodes, which nothing surveyed does today.
pitfalls: Observer/instrumentation overhead skewing the very measurement being taken: patching every CanvasRenderingContext2D method to capture a stack trace or push a log entry on every call is fine at tens of calls/frame but becomes the dominant cost at the thousands-of-calls/frame scale common in charting (each drawImage call has ~3-9.5us of inherent binding overhead per browser per public benchmarks, and adding a stack capture or object allocation on top can multiply that). Mitigate by counting/timing per-frame batches rather than per-call, and by sampling (e.g. full command capture only 1 frame in N) rather than capturing every frame.

GPU work is asynchronous relative to CPU-side JS: a wrapped gl.drawArrays()/drawElements() call returns almost instantly because it only enqueues work — the actual GPU execution happens later and out-of-band, so naive performance.now() timing around a draw call measures 'time to enqueue,' not 'time to render.' Real GPU cost requires EXT_disjoint_timer_query (WebGL) or timestamp-query (WebGPU), both of which return results asynchronously (poll or await, sometimes a frame or more later) and can report DISJOINT=true (meaning throw the reading away) if the GPU's clock/power state changed mid-query — a tool that doesn't check the disjoint flag will silently report bogus numbers. Canvas2D has no equivalent extension at all; 2D context timing is CPU-side-only by necessity since there's no exposed GPU command queue to instrument.

React StrictMode double-invocation in development: components, and specifically render-phase code plus certain effects, run twice per commit in dev-only StrictMode to surface impure side effects. A canvas draw triggered from a component body or an effect will fire twice for what is, in production, a single logical commit — any redundant-draw detector built and tested only in dev will systematically over-count 'redundant' redraws unless it's aware of StrictMode's mount->unmount->mount double-invoke pattern, or the tool is validated against a production build (where the double-invoke doesn't happen) before trusting its counts.

Attribution heuristics (timestamp-window correlation, stack-frame parsing) are inherently approximate, not causal: React exposes no direct pointer from 'this commit' to 'this imperative side effect ran because of it' for arbitrary DOM refs/canvas writes — unlike prop/state diffs which React tracks natively. Multiple components committing in the same batch, or a canvas draw deferred to a later rAF/microtask rather than firing synchronously in a layout effect, will break naive time-window bucketing and misattribute the draw to the wrong (or no) commit. Treat any automatic attribution as a hint to verify, not ground truth — a manual opt-in reporting hook (component calls into the profiler with its own name) remains the only fully reliable channel.

Canvas layers owned by third-party charting/graphics libraries (Konva, PixiJS, Fabric, D3-on-canvas, or an internal LineChart/MetricsGraphCanvas wrapper) often run their own internal render loop and dirty-tracking decoupled from React's render cycle entirely — a rAF callback registered once in a mount effect and left running independently. Global prototype-patching still sees these draws (since it patches the underlying context, not React), but 'attributing to a component' is meaningless once the library's own scheduler is driving the loop; the tool needs to distinguish 'canvas draws driven synchronously by a React commit' from 'canvas draws driven by an independent internal loop that a commit merely started/stopped' — conflating them will misreport an animating chart as constantly re-rendering-due-to-React when the actual React-caused cost was a single effect that started the loop once.

Frame-command hashing/diffing for redundancy detection has its own cost/precision tradeoff: hashing a full command stream (all args of every call) per frame is expensive if done naively (stringifying floating-point args, deep-hashing image/pixel arguments) and can itself become slower than the redraw it's trying to flag as redundant; but a cheap hash (e.g. just call count + method name sequence) will produce false negatives (same call count/sequence, different argument values still shows a visual change) or false positives (functionally-identical draws using different float precision/NaN-adjacent values hash differently). Dirty-rect-based approaches sidestep exact-command comparison but require the app to expose region bounds, which most canvas code doesn't track explicitly.

OffscreenCanvas + Worker rendering breaks main-thread-only instrumentation entirely: if a component transfers control of the canvas to a worker, all prototype patches installed on the main thread's CanvasRenderingContext2D/WebGL*RenderingContext become irrelevant for that canvas, since the worker has its own global scope and its own (unpatched, unless separately instrumented) context classes. A drop-in tool has to either patch inside the worker too (requiring the app to load the instrumentation script in the worker context, defeating pure drop-in-ness) or fall back to only the coarse postMessage-based signals crossing the thread boundary.
